one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban joins Senate President Drilon, Speaker Belmonte, and the Inquirer's own Feb. 13 editorial 'Of the highest urgency' in urging speedy resolution of the Grace Poe eligibility cases, but redirects part of the critical gaze to the Comelec. He first outlines graduated dark scenarios: if Poe is disqualified BEFORE the election, votes for her will still be counted by the automated machines (programmed to count all printed-ballot names) but boards of canvassers may be barred from canvassing them -- though 'in this age of computers, geeks could still compute the results'; if AFTER the election and canvass but she fails to win, no problem; if AFTER she wins by highest votes, the second-placer would still be proclaimed, spawning political troubles; if AFTER she is proclaimed and AFTER she assumes office, only an election contest at the PET resolves the crisis. The unifying lesson: only NOT disqualifying her avoids dark scenarios. He then defends the SC: CJ Sereno publicly prioritized election cases; oral argument closed with a six-day memo deadline comparable to FPJ's pace. By contrast, he notes the disqualification suits against Rodrigo Duterte remain unresolved at the Comelec en banc -- so dark scenarios persist for him too. He builds two contrasting precedent timelines. Estrada's 2010 case slept in the Comelec for months (Second Division dismissal Jan 10, en banc denial May 4 -- less than a week before election day) and reached the SC only on May 7; the Court dismissed as moot in Pormento vs Comelec (Aug 31, 2010) because Estrada lost. (He notes Vidal vs Comelec, Jan 21, 2015, later held that Estrada's absolute pardon restored his right to seek public office.) FPJ's 2004 case was lightning-fast: petition filed Jan 9, Comelec First Division dismissal Jan 23, en banc affirmance Feb 6, SC Tecson decision March 3 -- Comelec en banc dismissal was 'noteworthy for its deep sleep' in Estrada's case, FPJ's for its 'blinding speed.' In both cases neither candidate was disqualified, the electorate had freedom of choice, votes were counted, and no dark scenarios occurred. The Comelec's asymmetric treatment is striking: it included Estrada on the ballots but cancelled Poe's COC. He closes with confident institutional faith: the Court 'will come up with a speedy and fair decision that will avoid the gruesome constitutional and political crises that critics fear.'
